extracted.intended_audience: general public; students, journalists, and legal/policy researchers interested in federal appointments law
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and application of the Federal Vacancies Reform Act of 1998: who may serve as acting officers, how long they may serve, statutory exceptions, reporting requirements, and related constitutional and case-law constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope — offices covered by the Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Applies to 'an appointed office of an executive agency of the government' (defined to include the Executive Office of the President and exclude the GAO) and to any affected office for which an advice-and-consent appointment is required, subject to listed exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act governs temporary filling of vacant executive agency positions that require presidential appointment with Senate confirmation, but some offices are exempt where another statute expressly supersedes or provides an alternative designation process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggering events for vacancy
rubrics_metrics.description: When an appointed officer of an executive agency dies, resigns, or is otherwise unable to perform office functions, the Act's procedures for temporary appointment are triggered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vacancy can be actual death/resignation or inability to perform functions; the Act imposes time limits and eligibility rules once a vacancy exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default succession — first assistant rule
rubrics_metrics.description: By default, 'the first assistant to the office' becomes the acting officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute retains the requirement that the first assistant shall perform the functions temporarily in an acting capacity, subject to the time limitations of the Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate eligible class — Senate-confirmed personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may direct a person currently serving in a different Senate-confirmed position to serve as acting officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows temporary reassignments of other confirmed officers to perform the vacant office's functions for the statutory period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate eligible class — senior agency employee
rubrics_metrics.description: The President can select a senior 'officer or employee' of the same executive agency who is equivalent to a GS-15 or above on the federal pay scale, provided that employee served in that agency for at least 90 days during the 365 days preceding the end of the previous Senate-confirmed officeholder's service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often referred to as the 'senior officer or employee' clause; has been the subject of constitutional debate when applied to principal officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent nominee restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: A person nominated to a position may not concurrently serve as an acting officer for that position unless that person is in a 'first assistant' position to that office and either has served in that position for at least 90 days, or was appointed to that position through the advice and consent process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents nominees from simultaneously acting in the office except in narrow circumstances (first assistant with 90+ days' service or Senate-confirmed appointment to the first assistant role).

rubrics_metrics.name: General term limit for acting service (210 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a vacancy occurs, the position can be filled by an acting officer for 210 days from the date of the vacancy, in addition to the time when a nomination is pending before the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 210-day clock governs most vacancy situations; time during which a nomination is pending also counts toward allowable acting service in particular ways described by the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incoming President extended term (300 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: An incoming President is given 300 days in which to temporarily and unilaterally fill positions with 'acting' officers (instead of the regular 210 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a longer initial period after presidential transitions; the article elsewhere characterizes this as allowing newly elected presidents 300 days to appoint acting officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of nominations on term limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If a first or second nomination is rejected by the Senate or withdrawn, it activates additional 210-day periods from the date of the rejection or withdrawal, but this does not apply to a third or later nomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejection/withdrawal of the first two nominations extends the acting-authority timeline; third and later nominations do not trigger further 210-day extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When vacancy persists after timing limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If an office remains vacant after 210 days after the rejection, withdrawal, or return of a second presidential appointment nomination, it remains vacant until a person is appointed by the President by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. In such instance, only the head of an executive agency may perform office functions until such appointment is made in the case of an office other than the office of head of an executive agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute restricts who may perform the functions once the allowable acting period and nomination-triggered extensions have been exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: No effect clause for violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Any action to perform a function of a vacant office by a person filling a vacancy in violation of requirements or by a person who is not filling such vacancy shall have no effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments or actions taken by persons serving outside the Act's eligibility/timing rules can be void; courts and GAO may treat such acts as without legal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exceptions and superseding provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The vacancy and time limitation provisions do not apply where: (1) another statutory provision expressly supersedes such provisions, or (2) a statutory provision in effect on the Act's enactment date expressly authorizes the President, a court, or the head of an executive department to designate an officer to perform the functions temporarily in an acting capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain agency-specific statutes (e.g., Homeland Security Act, Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act) set alternative succession processes that override the FVRA for particular offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess appointments and alternative appointment mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Recess appointments by the President and other constitutionally authorized appointment mechanisms operate alongside or as exceptions to the FVRA in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act does not eliminate the President's ability to make recess appointments where constitutional authority permits; interplay between FVRA and recess-appointment power is a legal consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency-specific exceptions (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain statutes or provisions provide explicit exceptions—e.g., Homeland Security Act (under secretary of homeland security for management as third in succession), Intelligence Reform Act (principal deputy director of national intelligence first in line), Federal Judicial Code as applied to the Attorney General, and a separate law for the Secretary of Labor with no time limit on acting service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples show that Congress can and has legislated alternative succession rules or removed time limits for specific offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting requirements to Congress and GAO
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires executive branch departments and agencies to report to Congress and the Government Accountability Office information about temporary filling of vacant executive agency positions that require presidential appointment with Senate confirmation; Comptroller General must report to specified congressional committees, the President, and OPM if an acting officer is determined to be serving longer than the 210 days (including applicable exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates transparency and oversight mechanisms intended to track compliance with FVRA limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lines of succession planning requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act mandated that federal departments and agencies create lines of succession plans in case of disaster or emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many agencies did not fulfill this requirement until after 9/11; the statute spurred executive orders and formalized succession practices in departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional constraints — Appointments Clause and principal vs inferior officers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an argument (and litigation history) that the 'senior officer or employee' clause may be unconstitutional when applied to principal officers because the Appointments Clause requires Senate confirmation for principal officers; OLC opinion under the George W. Bush administration held that all acting officers are inferior officers and thus not subject to the advice-and-consent requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and jurists disagree; Supreme Court and lower-court decisions (and OLC opinions) shape how the FVRA is applied to principal vs inferior officer questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal consequences and judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Court rulings and GAO determinations can find particular acting appointments unlawful (examples include rulings invalidating appointments such as L.M.-M. v. Cuccinelli and rulings that certain officials are serving in violation of the FVRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments found unlawful can invalidate directives and agency actions taken while the person served; litigation and GAO reports are mechanisms for enforcement and clarification of the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special provisions for inaugural transitions and independent establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: The law sets forth additional provisions regarding vacancies existing during presidential inaugural transitions, independent establishments, and exceptions for certain board members of independent establishments or government corporations or commissioners of FERC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FVRA includes tailored rules for transition periods and for certain independent entities, reflecting different policy and statutory treatment across agency types.
